Brisbane's steep inner suburbs and wider foothill blocks pose different access problems, but both benefit from an accurate retained-height record and an outlet plan for collected water. Start with wide photos and rough measurements. Note cracks, leaning, decayed posts, erosion, wet areas and recent changes above the wall. This evidence helps distinguish a material preference from the actual site problem. What a Brisbane retaining wall has to hold back A retaining wall carries three things at once: the weight of the soil behind it, the water moving through that soil, and whatever sits on the ground above. The first two are constant. The third is the one property owners most often forget, because a driveway, a carport slab, a pool shell or a neighbour's shed reads as part of the yard rather than as a load pressing on a structure a metre away. That is why retained height, measured from the base of the wall to the finished soil level behind it, is the single most useful number to establish early. It sets the pressure the wall must resist, and in Queensland it also sits close to the threshold where an exemption stops applying. A wall that looks 800 millimetres tall from the lawn can be 1.4 metres from the footing once the buried courses are counted. Water is the usual reason walls fail Saturated backfill weighs more than dry backfill and exerts a hydrostatic push that most walls were never sized for. Brisbane's summer storm pattern delivers that condition in short, intense bursts rather than steadily, so a wall can stand for years and then move in a single wet fortnight. The classic Brisbane sequence is a broken or redirected downpipe feeding the retained zone, followed by fines washing out through a joint, followed by a visible dip in the ground above. A working drainage system is a connected path, not a length of slotted pipe thrown into the trench. Water enters through clean aggregate protected by a filter fabric matched to the local soil, travels along a graded subsoil line, and leaves at an outlet that is visible, lawful and maintainable. A pipe that simply disappears into the ground has not shown where the water goes. Approvals, licensing and who signs what Brisbane City Council describes limited circumstances in which a retaining wall may be built without building approval, and the Queensland Development Code sets the deemed-to-satisfy conditions behind them. Height is only the first test. Surcharge loads above the wall, proximity to another wall or a building, boundary position, easements, overlays and protected vegetation each apply separately, and any one of them can pull an otherwise simple wall into the approval pathway. Where design is required, it comes from an engineer registered with the Board of Professional Engineers of Queensland, and the certification trail runs on Form 15 for the design and Form 16 for the inspection and compliance of the built work. Construction itself is regulated building work above the statutory value threshold, so the contractor should hold a QBCC licence covering the class of work. The QBCC licence search is public and worth using before a deposit is paid. Turning observations into a scope A quotation
